title: Variables
intro: Distinguish observational units from variables, classify categorical and quantitative data, and separate statistics from parameters.

moments.title: Observational units
moments.text: The unit is the individual item from which information is recorded.

moments.title: Variables
moments.text: A variable can differ across observational units.

moments.title: Quantitative variables
moments.text: Values measure or count a quantity.

moments.title: Discrete values
moments.text: A discrete variable has countable possible values.

moments.title: Continuous values
moments.text: A continuous variable can take any value in an interval.

moments.title: Population parameters
moments.text: A numerical population summary is a parameter.

moments.title: Sample statistics
moments.text: A numerical sample summary is a statistic.

moments.title: Samples vary
moments.text: Different samples can produce different statistics.

cards.name: Unit or variable?
cards.text: The unit is what is observed. The variable is what is recorded about it.

cards.name: Label or quantity?
cards.text: Numerical category codes are still labels; arithmetic on them is not meaningful.

cards.name: Discrete or continuous?
cards.text: Counts have countable possibilities; idealized measurements vary continuously.

cards.name: Parameter or statistic?
cards.text: Check whether the summary describes the whole population or a sample.

questions.q: For each mug, record material, capacity in milliliters, and number of printed logos. Identify the unit and classify each variable.

work.text: Each mug is one observational unit.
Material is categorical. Capacity and number of logos are quantitative.
Capacity is continuous; the number of logos is discrete.

questions.answer: A numerical-looking value is quantitative only when it represents a meaningful measured or counted quantity.

traps.title: Numerical labels
traps.weak: A postcode is quantitative because it uses digits.
traps.better: A postcode labels a location and is categorical.

traps.title: Count versus measurement
traps.weak: Recorded height is discrete because we round it.
traps.better: Height is modeled as continuous even when recorded to a fixed precision.

traps.title: Unit versus variable
traps.weak: The observational unit is the number of logos.
traps.better: The mug is the unit; its number of logos is a variable.

traps.title: Population versus sample
traps.weak: A mean is always a parameter.
traps.better: A mean is a parameter for a population and a statistic for a sample.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Category names can be numerical codes. Classify the meaning of a variable rather than deciding from whether its values look like words or numbers. A discrete variable need not have only finitely many possible values.

questions.stem: A warehouse records parcel ID, mass, and number of items for each parcel. Which is categorical?
why: The item count is quantitative and discrete.
The ID is a label, even if it is numeric.
A mean summarizes a quantitative variable.

questions.stem: Which variable is quantitative and discrete?
opts: Time needed to read a message
why: A count has countable possible values.

questions.stem: The mean mass of all 600 parcels shipped today is known. This number is a:
why: Mass is the variable; the mean is a summary.
It summarizes the entire population of today's parcels.
A sample is a collection of units.

questions.stem: Why might two random samples of customers have different mean waiting times?
opts: One mean must be a parameter
why: Random samples need not give identical results.
Different customers have different waiting times.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A wildlife center samples 45 rescued birds from its full register. For each bird it records an identification code, wing length, and number of previous admissions. The sample mean wing length is 24 cm.
parts: (a) Identify the observational unit and classify the three variables.
(b) Is 24 cm a parameter or statistic? Explain.
(c) Identify the corresponding population parameter and explain why another sample could give a different result.
sample: (a) One rescued bird is the unit. The identification code is categorical; wing length is continuous quantitative; the number of previous admissions is discrete quantitative.
(b) 24 cm is a statistic because it summarizes the 45 sampled birds.
(c) The parameter is the mean wing length of all birds in the full register. Another sample can contain different birds with different wing lengths.
checklist: Identifies one bird as the unit.
Classifies the identification code as categorical.
Distinguishes continuous length from discrete count.
Calls 24 cm a sample statistic with a reason.
Names the population mean and explains variation.
